traveler: Abu Abdallah Muhammad ibn Battuta (Ibn Battuta al-Lawati al-Tanji)
title: The Vow Against Repeating a Road: Tangier to the Niger by way of Delhi, Zaitun, and the Kaaba
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Tangier, birth in a house of qadis
stops.date_confidence: attested: Britannica and Encyclopedia.com give 24 February 1304, 703 AH
stops.campa: In the year 703 of the Hijra a son is born at Tangier into a family of Maliki qadis, and the boy is set to the family trade: Qur'an, hadith, and the law of Malik, the preparation every judge in the western Maghreb takes before he is trusted with a court. No record says when that schooling ends. What the record gives instead is a departure date, and a vow he makes to himself before he has anything to measure it against: never to travel the same road twice.
suggested_refs: The Maliki qadi's curriculum of fourteenth-century Tangier, and the Great Mosque quarter of his birth

stops.name: Tangier, the departure alone
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: the Rihla's own opening line, 2 Rajab 725
stops.campa: He is twenty-one and he rides out alone, without companion and without caravan, on the road every Muslim of the Maghreb knows by name and few take. He means to make the hajj and to study under whatever scholars the road produces along the way. He will be gone twenty-four years, and within months of coming home he will leave again for the desert. The vow against repeating a road turns one pilgrimage into an itinerary of three continents, and the book will spend twenty-nine years testing it.
stops.quote: I left Tangier, my birthplace, on Thursday, 2nd Rajab 725 [June 14, 1325]
stops.quote_source: Rihla, opening line, trans. H. A. R. Gibb, Travels in Asia and Africa 1325-1354 (1929), via Fordham Internet History Sourcebooks
suggested_refs: The eastward pilgrim road out of Tangier, taken alone in June 1325
sources: Gibb 1929, via Fordham Internet History Sourcebooks

stops.name: Alexandria, the lighthouse with one side fallen
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year only; month unrecorded, defaulted
stops.campa: He crosses North Africa by Tunis, where the pilgrim caravan makes him its qadi and where he weeps among strangers until one of them consoles him, and reaches Alexandria some three thousand five hundred kilometres from home. The Pharos still stands with one side collapsed. He walks the ruin, measures what is left of it, and sets down the harbor as one of the great ports of the world. Emir Abdelkader will be initiated into a lodge on this same shore in 1864.
suggested_refs: The ruined Pharos of Alexandria as Ibn Battuta found it, one side already down

stops.name: Fuwwa, the hermit who names three brothers
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the visit follows Alexandria in the Rihla's order; no month or day is given, and the Fuwwa coordinates are the town, not the hermitage
stops.campa: South of Alexandria, at Fuwwa in the Delta, he turns aside to the hermitage of Shaykh Burhan al-Din al-Murshidi and is given a bed and a prophecy: that he is bound for India, for Sind, and for China, and that in each country he will find one of the shaykh's brothers, Farid al-Din, Rukn al-Din, Burhan al-Din. The young man has not yet been as far as Cairo. All three meetings appear later in the book, in that order, exactly as foretold. The book is dictated thirty years afterward.
suggested_refs: The hermitage of Shaykh Burhan al-Din al-Murshidi at Fuwwa in the Nile Delta
sources: verification note correcting the pool's placement of al-Murshidi at Alexandria

stops.name: Cairo, the mother of cities
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the Rihla gives no month for the first Cairo stay
stops.campa: He comes up the Delta into Cairo and cannot stop counting: twelve thousand water carriers, thirty thousand mules for hire, a river of people that will not fit inside the walls his eye gives it. He lodges among the students of al-Azhar and plans a route up the Nile to the Red Sea. Rebellion on the upper river closes that road, and he turns back north to take the overland way through Syria instead. Al-Kamil ruled this city a century before him; the schools he sleeps in outlast the sultan.
stops.quote: I arrived at length at Cairo, mother of cities and seat of Pharaoh the tyrant, mistress of broad regions and fruitful lands, boundless in multitude of buildings, peerless in beauty and splendour, the meeting-place of comer and goer, the halting-place of feeble and mighty, whose throngs surge as the waves of the sea, and can scarce be contained in her for all her size and capacity.
stops.quote_source: Rihla, Cairo chapter, trans. H. A. R. Gibb, cited on Wikiquote and Fordham Internet History Sourcebooks
suggested_refs: Mamluk Cairo and the student lodgings of al-Azhar in 1326
sources: Gibb translation, via Wikiquote and Fordham

stops.name: Jerusalem, the third sanctuary in passing
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Rihla records the visit on the Syrian road in 1326, but no reachable source in this pool dates it; the pin comes from the atlas interlock
stops.campa: On the Syrian road he turns aside to Jerusalem and prays at the Haram, on ground this atlas already crowds: al-Kamil who handed the city to Frederick by treaty, Ibn Arabi, Maimonides, Marco Polo, Richard of England. Ibn Battuta arrives as none of these, neither conqueror nor exile nor envoy, but as a pilgrim in transit with a caravan to catch. He prays at the Dome and at the Aqsa, notes the endowments that feed the city's poor, and goes north again toward Damascus.
suggested_refs: The Haram al-Sharif in 1326, between the Frankish century and the Ottoman one

stops.name: Damascus, the certificates and the caravan
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the Rihla places the arrival in Ramadan 726, conventionally August 1326
stops.campa: He reaches Damascus as the Syrian hajj caravan is forming. He prays in the Umayyad Mosque, which he says has no rival among the mosques of the world, sits with its scholars long enough to take certificates in hadith, and marries. The certificates are working capital: a man carrying Damascene isnads eats at madrasa tables from Anatolia to the Indus. Al-Kamil governed here a hundred years before. Ibn Battuta will stand in this courtyard again in 1348, in a city burying two thousand a day.
suggested_refs: The Umayyad Mosque of Damascus and the hadith certificates issued there in 1326

stops.name: Salihiyya, at the tomb of Ibn Arabi
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Rihla records the visit during the 1326 Damascus stay; no day is given and the stop reaches this file through the atlas interlock
stops.campa: On the slope of Mount Qasiyun, in Salihiyya outside the walls, he prays at the grave of Muhyi al-Din Ibn Arabi, the Andalusian dead eighty-six years, whom the Sufis call the Greatest Master. Five centuries on, Emir Abdelkader will pray at this same stone as a boy of eighteen and be laid beside it as an old man of seventy-four. Ibn Battuta stays a day and rejoins his caravan. The pilgrim road south keeps its own schedule and will not wait on anyone's devotion.
suggested_refs: The tomb of Ibn Arabi at Salihiyya, before Selim I built the mosque over it

stops.name: Medina, four days at the Prophet's tomb
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; ORIAS dates the Medina to Mecca leg to 1326, month approximate
stops.campa: The Syrian caravan comes down the pilgrim road to Medina, and he stands four days at the Prophet's tomb under the green dome, in the garden between pulpit and grave. He records the lamps, the custodians, the discipline of the enclosure, and the additions each sultan has paid for. He will pass through Medina on later pilgrimages and write down each time what has changed. Abdelkader will pray in this enclosure in 1825 with his father, and again alone in 1863.
suggested_refs: The Prophet's Mosque at Medina and the Rawda, as described in the Rihla

stops.name: Mecca, the first circuits of the Kaaba
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month: ORIAS gives the first pilgrimage completed in November 1326
stops.campa: The caravan comes into Mecca and he enters the sanctuary and makes the circuits, a Moroccan of twenty-two standing at the fixed point of the world. Nine journeys in this atlas have already touched this stone: Muhammad who cleared the idols from it, Rabia who came in 737, Nizami's father whose prayer failed here, Abraham before all of them, Abdelkader five centuries after. Ibn Battuta is the tenth, and he will be back three times. From here the road home runs west. He does not take it.
stops.quote: We immediately entered the holy sanctuary and began the rites of pilgrimage.
stops.quote_source: Rihla, Mecca chapter, trans. H. A. R. Gibb (1929), via Fordham Internet History Sourcebooks
suggested_refs: The Kaaba and the Grand Mosque, station of four separate stops in this journey

segments.name: The Caravan That Did Not Turn Home

stops.name: Mecca, the road to Iraq instead of the road west
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: ORIAS and Britannica give 17 November 1326 for the departure with the Iraq caravan
stops.campa: Seventeen days after the pilgrimage he attaches himself to a caravan forming for Iraq and rides north instead of west. Nothing compels it. The hajj is discharged, the vow is kept, and a qadi's post waits in Morocco for any man carrying Damascene certificates. He goes to Najaf instead, and from Najaf on to Basra, Isfahan, Shiraz, and Baghdad. The pilgrimage ends here and the journey begins here, and the whole difference between them is one caravan chosen on one morning.
suggested_refs: The Kufa road out of Mecca, taken by the Iraqi hajj caravan of 726 AH

stops.name: Najaf, the shrine that feeds a town
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the Rihla gives no month for the Najaf visit
stops.campa: At Najaf he enters the shrine of Ali ibn Abi Talib and describes what a Maliki lawyer from Tangier is under no obligation to admire: silver doors, carpets laid over carpets, gold and silver lamps burning above the sanctuary, a building he calls among the most magnificent in existence. He notes the Shia pilgrims crowding it, and under that the plain economic fact, that the town lives entirely on the shrine's endowments and would not exist a season without them.
suggested_refs: The shrine of Ali at Najaf and its endowments, as inventoried in the Rihla

stops.name: Baghdad, the bridge of boats
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month approximate, and the pin is the atlas's existing Baghdad pin rather than the Mustansiriya
stops.campa: Baghdad seventy years after the Mongols is two cities on two banks, joined by boats lashed together into a bridge, its Mustansiriya still teaching and its old splendor stripped off it. He meets the Ilkhanid Abu Sa'id's court on the march and travels with the royal camp a while before doubling back south for a second pilgrimage. Four centuries earlier al-Hallaj was executed in this city and his ashes thrown in this river. Abdelkader will kneel at the Jilani shrine here in 1826.
suggested_refs: The Mustansiriya madrasa and the pontoon bridge of post-Mongol Baghdad

stops.name: Mecca, the years of sitting still
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Encyclopedia.com gives roughly three resident years, 1327-1330; World History Encyclopedia instead places a third pilgrimage in the winter of 1330, and the sequence of the second and third hajj is not fixed
stops.campa: He comes back to Mecca and stays, by his own account given over to study, in the one city where a traveler can stop without admitting that he has stopped. He reads, keeps the pilgrimage seasons, and takes the certificates of Meccan shaykhs. It is the longest rest of his life until Delhi. When he moves again it is down to the Red Sea and the ships that run with the Yemeni monsoon, and after that not one year passes without a coast in it. He arrives at twenty-three and leaves at twenty-six, and no two sources agree on how many pilgrimages he keeps in between.
suggested_refs: The resident scholars of the Meccan sanctuary in the years around 1328

segments.name: Two Seas: the Swahili Coast and the Steppe

stops.name: Mogadishu, the meal written down as evidence
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the Rihla gives the monsoon season, not a month
stops.campa: He sails the Red Sea to Aden and takes the monsoon south down the African coast to Mogadishu, a city he calls exceedingly large, where the sultan's men meet every ship that arrives and no merchant picks his own host. He is fed as a visiting scholar is fed and he writes the meal down in detail, because the food of a place is evidence about the place. The Rihla is a lawyer's document as much as a traveler's: witnesses, hospitality, custom, and who pays for what.
stops.quote: Their food is rice cooked with ghee placed on a large wooden dish...
stops.quote_source: Ibn Battuta in Black Africa, trans. Said Hamdun and Noel King (Markus Wiener, 1994), p. 13
suggested_refs: The host-and-guest system of the Mogadishu harbor, in which arriving merchants were assigned their hosts

stops.name: Kilwa, the fifth part of the booty
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the Swahili leg is undated to the month in every reachable source
stops.campa: Further south at Kilwa he finds a stone town of well-built houses trading gold out of Sofala, and a sultan, Abu'l-Muzaffar Hasan, who raids the mainland and gives away a fifth of everything he takes, as the Book requires of him. Ibn Battuta approves in the exact register of a jurist checking compliance with a rule. From Kilwa he turns north again with the monsoon, by Oman and the Gulf, and comes back around to Mecca for another pilgrimage. The town's great mosque is roofed in coral stone quarried out of the reef the island sits on.
stops.quote: He used to devote the fifth part of the booty made on his expeditions to pious and charitable purposes, as is prescribed in the Koran
stops.quote_source: Rihla, on Sultan Abu'l-Muzaffar Hasan of Kilwa, trans. H. A. R. Gibb (1929), via World History Commons
suggested_refs: The stone town of Kilwa Kisiwani and the Sofala gold trade it lived on

stops.name: Konya, the tomb of Rumi and the akhi lodges
stops.date_confidence: contested: Wikipedia gives the Anatolia crossing as the autumn of 1330 or 1332, and this atlas's two research lenses split the same way; c.1330-31 is taken here and the conflict is not resolved
stops.campa: He crosses Anatolia, the country he calls Bilad al-Rum, and stops at Konya to visit the tomb of Jalal al-Din Rumi, whose followers take their name from him and turn as they pray. Across the whole region he is handed from one akhi lodge to the next: guilds of young craftsmen who compete for the right to feed a stranger and quarrel with each other over who gets him. He records the quarrels with pleasure. It is the most dependable hospitality he finds on any of the three continents.
suggested_refs: The akhi brotherhoods of fourteenth-century Anatolia, and the tomb of Rumi at Konya

stops.name: Kaffa, the first city of bells
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year in the chronology lens; the same leg is dated 1330 by the geography lens and the conflict is carried
stops.campa: At Kaffa in Genoese Crimea he lands in a town where bells ring instead of the call to prayer, the first such town of his life. He and his companions go up to the top of their lodging and answer with the adhan and with recitation, and the local Muslims come running to stop them, afraid of what the place will do about it. He sets down the bells and the fear together in one paragraph. From here he rides inland to find the moving court of the Golden Horde.
suggested_refs: Genoese Kaffa in the 1330s, a Black Sea port under Latin rule with a Muslim minority
sources: verification note correcting the minaret version of the episode

stops.name: Sarai on the Volga, the city that packs and moves
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year, contested as to site: his al-Sara is conventionally identified with Sarai Batu at Selitrennoye, and the pool's Sarai al-Jadid label and coordinates are rejected here
stops.campa: He joins the ordu, the traveling capital of Sultan Muhammad Uzbek Khan, and comes with it to al-Sara on the Volga: wagons, tents, markets, a khan's household that strikes and reloads as one body. He calls it among the finest cities in the world and rides its streets carefully, because the retinue's horses do not stop for a scholar on foot. Here he attaches himself to the party of a Byzantine-born khatun who is traveling home to her father to give birth.
suggested_refs: The Golden Horde ordu of Uzbek Khan, a capital carried on wagons
sources: verification note on the Sarai Batu and Sarai al-Jadid identifications

stops.name: Constantinople, the court of the other faith
stops.date_confidence: contested: Encyclopedia.com dates the visit to 1332, other accounts to 1334; neither is resolved here
stops.campa: With the khatun's retinue he passes the frontier and enters Constantinople, where he is received at the imperial court, questioned about Jerusalem, and shown the city. He counts monasteries, describes the great church from the outside, and declines to make the obeisance expected of him. It is one of very few Christian capitals in the book that he sees with his own eyes. When the khatun stays with her family, he turns back east across the steppe toward Khwarazm and the road to India.
suggested_refs: The Byzantine court of Andronikos III, as described by a Maghribi qadi in transit

stops.name: Bukhara, a tower standing in rubble
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the Transoxiana crossing is undated to the month
stops.campa: Bukhara a century after Genghis Khan is rubble with a tower in it. The mosques and madrasas are broken, the scholars scattered or dead, and the learning that once outshone every city of the Muslim east is reduced to whatever a traveler can find by asking in the street. The great minaret stands because the Mongols chose to leave it standing. He mourns the city in the past tense and rides on through Samarkand and the Khorasan passes toward the Hindu Kush and the winter road.
suggested_refs: The Kalyan minaret of Bukhara, spared in the Mongol destruction of 1220

stops.name: The Indus, the crossing into the Sultanate
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: Wikipedia gives 12 September 1333. The ford is not identified; the pin is a point on the river itself, correcting a pool coordinate that fell inside Multan
stops.campa: He comes down out of the snow with a hired caravan and crosses the Indus, the threshold of the Delhi Sultanate. On the far bank the sultan's intelligence officers take his name, his origin, his companions, and his purpose, and send the report ahead by courier. Muhammad bin Tughluq will know who is coming, and roughly what the man is worth to him, weeks before the man arrives. Ibn Battuta has entered a state that reads its own roads and writes down what it reads.
suggested_refs: The Delhi Sultanate's barid, the courier and intelligence service that reported every arrival at the frontier

stops.name: Delhi, qadi of the capital
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of arrival; the tenure is bracketed 1334 to 1341/42 and no source dates its individual years
stops.campa: Muhammad bin Tughluq receives him, gives him a house, villages for income, and the office of qadi of the capital on a salary that would keep a small court. The sultan collects foreign scholars the way other rulers collect horses. Ibn Battuta holds the post seven or eight years, judges through interpreters in a language he does not speak, spends past his income, and learns that the hand which pays this well also has men flayed in the maidan. He appears in no Delhi chronicle of the period.
suggested_refs: The Tughluqabad court of Muhammad bin Tughluq, and the silence of Barani and the Delhi chroniclers about its Maghribi qadi
sources: verification note on the absence of contemporary Delhi corroboration

stops.name: Delhi, the embassy that leaves and does not return
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year: Britannica and Wikipedia date the China embassy to 1341
stops.campa: The sultan names him ambassador to the Yuan court, with horses, slaves, robes, and swords for the emperor of China, and a Chinese embassy to escort home. The party is barely clear of the capital when bandits fall on it. He is cut off from his companions, stripped of everything he carries, and found days later alone. The mission goes on south through Gujarat toward the sea, and Ibn Battuta goes with it. He never sees Delhi or Muhammad bin Tughluq again.
suggested_refs: The 1341 Delhi embassy to the Yuan court, and the road robbery that opened it

stops.name: Calicut, the fleet broken in the roadstead
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the Rihla gives the day of the week, a Friday, but not the date
stops.campa: At Calicut the fleet loads and waits for its wind. He is ashore at Friday prayers when a storm comes into the harbor and breaks the ships on it: the emperor's gifts, the horses, the slaves, his own companions, all of it in the water while he watches from the beach with a prayer mat and a few dinars. To go back to Delhi with the sultan's property drowned is not a survivable report. He sails south instead, and stops being an ambassador without ever resigning.
suggested_refs: The Calicut roadstead of the Zamorin, where the Delhi embassy's fleet was wrecked

stops.name: Male, chief qadi of the atolls
stops.date_confidence: contested: arrival is placed around December 1343 with departure by August 1344, about nine months, while another lens asserts about eighteen; the claim that the ruling sultana appointed him collides with a king-list dating Khadijah's first reign to 1347-1362/63
stops.campa: Blown into the Maldive atolls, he is recognized as a trained Maliki jurist within days and cannot get out again: the islands have no qadi and the court does not release the one who arrives. He is appointed chief judge, married into the ruling family, and set to enforce prayer attendance and the veil on an island population that declines both. He has absentees whipped, loses the argument about the veil entirely, falls out with his in-laws, and takes ship.
stops.quote: It was customary with me, when acting as qazi in the Maldive islands, that whenever I sent for one of the party in a suit I sent him a blank or filled-in notice.
stops.quote_source: The Rehla of Ibn Battuta, trans. Mahdi Husain (Gaekwad's Oriental Series, Baroda, 1953/1976)
suggested_refs: The Hukuru Miskiy, the old Friday Mosque of Male, and the Maldivian court he married into

stops.name: Adam's Peak, the chains fixed in the rock
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the Ceylon ascent is undated to the month
stops.campa: In Ceylon he climbs the cone the pilgrims call Adam's Peak, hauling himself up the last stretch on iron chains driven into the rock by earlier climbers, to the hollow in the summit stone that Buddhists venerate as the Buddha's footprint and Muslims as Adam's. He calls the ascent one of the wonders of the world and notes that sailors see the peak far out at sea. Hermann Keyserling lands on this island in 1911 and writes his own chapter about it. He is put ashore twice on that coast, once by weather and once by a sultan who wants him.
stops.quote: When I entered the island of Ceylon I found that the inhabitants who were infidels respected the Muslim fakirs, gave them shelter in their houses and fed them.
stops.quote_source: The Rehla of Ibn Battuta, trans. Mahdi Husain (Gaekwad's Oriental Series, Baroda, 1953/1976)
suggested_refs: The pilgrim chains of Adam's Peak and the footprint shared by four religions

stops.name: Sylhet, the ascetic with one goat
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year for the Bengal leg; the identification of the shaykh is a reconstruction, not a date problem
stops.campa: In the Kamaru mountains beyond Bengal he climbs to a cave where an ascetic lives with one goat and nothing else, and stays with him. He gives the man's name as Jalal al-Din al-Tabrizi and reports that the shaykh knew he was coming and had sent someone down to meet him. Bengal itself he calls a hell full of good things, meaning the rice is cheap and the air is bad. The shrine tradition of Sylhet names that ascetic Shah Jalal and keeps the meeting as its own founding scene.
suggested_refs: The dargah of Shah Jalal at Sylhet, and the Gulzar-i-Abrar of 1613 that supplied its miracles
sources: verification note on the Jalal al-Din al-Tabrizi identification

stops.name: Barahnakar, the coast of the dog-mouthed men
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and contested as to place: the Rihla gives no date here, and the stop is dated with the Bengal and Sumatra legs that bracket it, fifteen days' sail out of Sonargaon by the book's own count and twenty-five days short of Sumatra. Gibb (1929, p. 366 n. 1) follows Yule in rejecting the older Andaman and Nicobar identifications for the Arakan mainland near the island of Negrais; Beckingham (Hakluyt Society IV, 1994, p. 874 n. 1) calls the people not satisfactorily identified, notes that elephants and a resident Muslim quarter rule out both island groups, and puts the landfall somewhere near Cape Negrais. The pin is Cape Negrais, not an attested landing. Gibb and Beckingham both read Barahnakar as the name of a people rather than of a country
stops.campa: Fifteen days out of Sonargaon the junk touches a coast where, he writes, the men have the mouths of dogs and the women do not. He records it the way he records a market: reed huts roofed with grass, banana and areca and betel, water carried to the ships on elephants because the wells lie inland and no merchant is let near them, elephants sold by the sultan alone and only for cloth. Among these people he finds a quarter of Muslims out of Bengal and Sumatra. Ratramnus of Corbie had ruled five centuries earlier that such men could be baptized.
stops.quote: Fifteen days after leaving Sunarkawan we reached the country of the Barahnakar, whose mouths are like those of dogs. This tribe is a rabble, professing neither the religion of the Hindus nor any other. They live in reed huts roofed with grasses on the seashore, and have abundant banana, areca, and betel trees. Their men are shaped like ourselves, except that their mouths are shaped like those of dogs; this is not the case with their womenfolk, however, who are endowed with surpassing beauty. Their men too go unclothed, not even hiding their nakedness, except occasionally for an ornamental pouch of reeds suspended from their waists. The women wear aprons of leaves of trees. With them reside a number of Muslims from Bengal and Sumatra, who occupy a separate quarter. The natives do all their trafficking with the merchants on the shore, and bring them water on elephants, because the water is at some distance from the coast and they will not let the merchants go to draw it for themselves, fearing for their women because they make advances to well-formed men. Elephants are numerous in their land, but no one may dispose of them except the sultan, from whom they are bought in exchange for woven stuffs.
stops.quote_source: Rihla, chapter X, trans. H. A. R. Gibb, Travels in Asia and Africa 1325-1354 (The Broadway Travellers, Routledge, 1929), p. 272. The web text of this passage, including Wikipedia's, reads 'Sunaridwan'; the printed Gibb reads 'Sunarkawan', which is Sonargaon in Bengal, and that reading is restored here
suggested_refs: The Arakan coast near Cape Negrais, where Yule and Gibb place the Barahnakar landfall
sources: Gibb 1929, pp. 271-272 and p. 366 n. 1, verified against the scanned edition
The Travels of Ibn Battuta AD 1325-1354, vol. IV, trans. Gibb and C. F. Beckingham (Hakluyt Society, 1994), p. 874 and n. 1
Henry Yule, Cathay and the Way Thither, IV, p. 92
san_cristobal.journey.json (the cynocephali and the Ratramnus ruling)

stops.name: Samudera Pasai, a Shafi'i court at the end of the ocean
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; coordinates reconciled between two lenses that disagreed by about thirteen kilometres
stops.campa: On the northern tip of Sumatra the sultan of Samudera Pasai receives him for a fortnight with royal honors. The court follows the Shafi'i school, keeps Arabic-speaking jurists, and wages war on its non-Muslim neighbors inland. A Moroccan lawyer finds the entire apparatus of a Muslim state working at the far end of the Indian Ocean, further from Mecca than he has ever stood. The sultan gives him a junk, provisions, and the wind for the South China Sea.
suggested_refs: The sultanate of Samudera Pasai, the earliest Muslim state in the Indonesian archipelago

stops.name: Quanzhou, landfall at Zaitun
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year for the landfall; everything narrated inland of this port is contested, and Dunn calls the question probably unsolvable
stops.campa: He makes landfall in China at the harbor the Arabs call Zaitun, and finds it crowded with junks, with a Muslim quarter, a qadi of its own, and Sufi lodges to put him up. Silk and porcelain leave from here for the whole world. Marco Polo saw this port forty years earlier and called it Zaiton. Of everything in the Rihla, the China chapters are the ground on which the book is most often accused of being a compilation rather than a journey. He records the porcelain kilns, the paper money, and the painters who copy a stranger's face.
stops.quote: I never returned to any of their cities after I had visited it a first time without finding my portrait and the portraits of my companions drawn on the walls and on sheets of paper exhibited in the bazaars.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Rihla, China chapter, trans. H. A. R. Gibb, on the painters of Zaytun; wording not verified against the primary translation in this pass
suggested_refs: The Qingjing Mosque quarter of Quanzhou and its resident Muslim merchant community under the Yuan
sources: Ross E. Dunn, The Adventures of Ibn Battuta (1986)

stops.name: Hangzhou, the largest city he has seen
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the inland Chinese itinerary is dated 1345-46 in the sources that accept it, and several modern historians suspect compression or borrowing in this leg
stops.campa: He describes coming inland to Hangzhou and calls it the largest city he has ever seen on the face of the earth, cut through with canals like Baghdad's but greater, with a Muslim quarter that hosts him and an official who feeds his whole party for three days. Marco Polo called the same city Quinsai and said much the same thing about it. Whether Ibn Battuta stood in these streets, or built them out of the accounts of men who had, is the oldest argument about his book.
suggested_refs: The canals of Yuan Hangzhou, described by both of the atlas's great medieval travelers

stops.name: Guangzhou, the river harbor and the turn
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: dated with the rest of the Chinese itinerary, and disputed with it; the claimed onward journey to Khanbaliq is doubted by modern historians
stops.campa: He describes Guangzhou on its great river, a walled city with a resident Muslim community, a mosque, a hospital, and a quarter given over to potters, and he claims a further journey north to Khanbaliq that the rest of the book cannot carry. Hermann Keyserling comes through this same port in 1911 with a philosopher's questions and a return ticket. From here the Rihla turns around: Sumatra, the Malabar coast, Quilon, and the long haul back across the Arabian Sea.
suggested_refs: The Canton foreign quarter under the Yuan, and the disputed Khanbaliq leg of the Rihla

stops.name: Damascus, the fast of three days
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: the plague chapter's Friday procession is dated 21 July 1348
stops.campa: He comes back into Damascus in July and finds the city under the plague. The governor orders a fast of three days, and on the Friday the whole population walks out together to the Mosque of the Footprints, Muslims and Jews and Christians, barefoot, carrying their books, from after dawn until past noon. He counts two thousand dead in a day at the worst of it. Twenty-two years earlier he took his hadith certificates in this city, and married here, and moved on.
stops.quote: the city's inhabitants should fast three days and come out on Friday to implore God to raise the plague from their city
stops.quote_source: Rihla, plague chapter, as cited in The Maydan and in academic treatments of the passage
suggested_refs: The Masjid al-Aqdam procession of 21 July 1348, the Rihla's eyewitness page on the Black Death
sources: academic treatments of the Rihla's plague chapter

stops.name: Mecca, the last circuits
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the stay of more than four months is attested, the month of arrival is approximate
stops.campa: He goes down by Jerusalem, Gaza, and Cairo to Jeddah and makes his final pilgrimage, staying more than four months in Mecca while the plague works forward through the Hejaz caravans behind him. The Kaaba is where the journey began twenty-two years ago and it is the last time he will stand at it. From here the road runs west, through an Egypt and a Maghreb emptying of people, toward a Tangier he last saw as a young man of twenty-one. He is forty-four years old and has been away from the Maghreb for twenty-three of them.
suggested_refs: The plague-year hajj of 1348 and the mortality among the Hejaz caravans
sources: academia.edu, 'A Two-year Journey under the Arrows of the Black Death'

stops.name: Fez, the Marinid court after twenty-four years
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month: the Rihla's own date, Sha'ban 750 AH, conventionally October or November 1349
stops.campa: He lands in the Maghreb and comes to Fez, capital of the Marinid sultan Abu Inan Faris, home after twenty-four years and the last stretch of it through Tunis and Algiers. He praises the sultan, the city, and the Maghreb in the formal register a returning subject owes his ruler, and he means it: after eight years under Muhammad bin Tughluq he has a standard of comparison for arbitrary power. Ibn Arabi taught at this city's Qarawiyyin, and Maimonides studied here.
suggested_refs: The Marinid capital of Fez in 1349, and the court of Abu Inan Faris
sources: academic summary citing the Rihla's Sha'ban 750 date

stops.name: Tangier, the house without his mother
stops.date_confidence: contested order: one lens has him reach Tangier first in 1349, the standard itinerary puts Fez first in Sha'ban 750 and Tangier after; the second order is followed here
stops.campa: He rides north to Tangier and learns that his mother died of the plague a few months before he landed, his father some years before that. The house is standing and the family is not in it. He stays a short while, crosses to al-Andalus in the spring, and is gone again inside the year. Twenty-four years on the road have made coming home a thing he can only do briefly. The vow against repeating a road turns out to cover the road back to his own door.
suggested_refs: The plague mortality in Tangier of 1348-49, which took his mother before his return

segments.name: The Salt Road and the Mansa

stops.name: Granada, the scholar who will write the book
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the Rihla gives no month for the Andalusian journey
stops.campa: He crosses to Nasrid Granada, the last Muslim kingdom in Iberia, in a season when the Castilian raids and the plague have both slackened. Sultan Yusuf is ill and does not receive him, and the sultan's mother pays for his stay out of her own purse. He sits instead with the scholars of the city, among them a young Granadan man of letters named Ibn Juzayy al-Kalbi, who will one day take down his book at Fez. Neither of them knows that yet. He crosses back to Morocco before the summer and begins asking about the road south.
suggested_refs: Nasrid Granada in 1350, and the first meeting of Ibn Battuta with his future scribe
sources: verification note correcting the Alhambra court reception

stops.name: Sijilmasa, the last town before the sand
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month: ORIAS gives the departure from Sijilmasa in February 1352
stops.campa: He goes south from Fez to Sijilmasa on the desert's edge, the last town before the sand, and lodges with the brother of a man who had hosted him in China. He buys camels, pastures them four months, and leaves in February with a caravan loaded with slabs of salt. In the Sudan those slabs trade weight for weight against gold dust. The Saharan road is a market with a distance in the middle of it, and the distance is what makes the price. The salt comes up out of pits at Taghaza, ten days out, cut in slabs a camel can carry two of.
suggested_refs: The Sijilmasa caravan of February 1352 and the salt-for-gold trade it carried

stops.name: Walata, the gift he takes for an insult
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month: ORIAS gives the arrival at Walata in April 1352
stops.campa: Twenty-five days across the sand, past the salt town of Taghaza whose houses and mosque are cut out of salt blocks, the caravan reaches Walata, the northern gate of the Mali empire. The welcome gift sent to him is a bowl of grain with a little honey and milk, and he reads it as contempt and writes so, in language about black Africans that he revises before he leaves the country. He also finds Massufa women who take lovers openly and jurists who do not object.
suggested_refs: Walata, the Massufa gateway town of the Mali empire, and the reception gift of 1352
sources: verification note on the misquoted 'no good' fragment

stops.name: Niani, the court of Mansa Sulayman
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the month is approximate, and the identification of the Malian capital with Niani is an archaeological reconstruction
stops.campa: He reaches the court of Mansa Sulayman and falls seriously ill within days of arriving, on a diet of millet and water, and is two months recovering. When he is well he complains to the mansa's face that other kings gave him more. He also sets down what he finds there: roads a lone traveler walks without fear, no seizure of a dead foreigner's goods, prayers kept in full, and children left in chains until they have the Qur'an by heart. He stays eight months and leaves owed nothing and owing nothing, which he counts as a slight.
stops.quote: of all people they are the furthest from injustice
stops.quote_source: Ibn Battuta in Black Africa, trans. Said Hamdun and Noel King (Markus Wiener, 1994), p. 58
suggested_refs: The court of Mansa Sulayman of Mali, and the Rihla's inventory of its justice and its slavery

stops.name: Timbuktu, the river and the boy
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the Niger leg is undated to the month
stops.campa: He goes down to the Niger and along it to Timbuktu, a river town under Mali's authority, smaller than the capital and valuable as the point where the gold road meets the caravan road. A companion pulls him back from the water's edge and explains, afterward, what lives in the river. At his departure he is given a boy, and he records the gift in the same voice he uses for camels and cloth. The boy is still in his household when the book is dictated.
stops.quote: The boy he gave me is still with me up till now
stops.quote_source: Ibn Battuta in Black Africa, trans. Said Hamdun and Noel King (Markus Wiener, 1994), p. 66
suggested_refs: The Djinguereber mosque and the Niger port of Timbuktu under Mali
sources: Yale Teachers Institute unit on Mansa Musa and Ibn Battuta

stops.name: Takadda, the last caravan north
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: ORIAS gives 11 September 1353; coordinates corrected to the Azelik wan Birni site
stops.campa: At Takadda in the copper country an order reaches him from Sultan Abu Inan to come home, and on the eleventh of September he leaves with a large caravan of merchants and slaves going north. He crosses by Hoggar and Tuat and comes into Sijilmasa in the winter, through snow he says is worse than anything he saw in Bukhara or Khwarazm. In January he is at Fez. The travel stops there, twenty-nine years after a young man rode east out of Tangier alone.
suggested_refs: The copper town of Takedda at Azelik wan Birni, and the September 1353 caravan north
sources: verification note correcting the Takadda coordinates

stops.name: Fez, the sultan orders the book taken down
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year for the commission; the dictation runs across 1355 into 1356
stops.campa: Abu Inan Faris orders the traveler's account written down and appoints Ibn Juzayy al-Kalbi, the Granadan scholar Ibn Battuta had met five years earlier, to do the writing. They work at Fez: one man talking his way through three continents from memory, his papers lost at sea off Calicut, and one man turning the talk into Arabic prose with verse set into the seams. They never travel together. Ibn Arabi and Maimonides both worked in this same mosque city.
suggested_refs: The Qarawiyyin of Fez, where the Rihla was dictated to Ibn Juzayy under Marinid commission

stops.name: Fez, the Gift completed
stops.date_confidence: contested: the colophon reads 756 AH, conventionally 1356, while some accounts date the finished written work to December 1355
stops.campa: Ibn Juzayy finishes the work and gives it the title it still carries, A Gift to Those who Contemplate the Wonders of Cities and the Marvels of Travelling. He dies within a year of finishing it. Nothing survives in either man's hand. Everything descends through later scribes, and the text the world now reads is rebuilt in Paris five centuries afterward out of manuscripts that French officers carried out of Constantine in the 1830s. Samuel Lee translates an abridgement in London in 1829, working from what had reached Cambridge.
suggested_refs: The five Constantine manuscripts taken to Paris in the 1830s, base of the Defremery and Sanguinetti edition of 1853-58
sources: Project MUSE, 'The Colonial Adventures of Confiscated Arabic Texts'

stops.name: Tangier, the room they show as his grave
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, three ways: the year is given as 1368 or 1369 and rarely 1377; the place as Marrakesh, as Tangier, or simply as Morocco. The pin is the traditional Tangier tomb, not an attested place of death, and the date is a placeholder
stops.campa: A small whitewashed room off a lane in the Tangier medina is shown as his grave, a stone under a cloth, the door usually locked. Nothing on it and nothing in any document says he is inside. He dies somewhere in Morocco while serving as a qadi in a town nobody names, buried by people who leave no record of it, and is read again outside the Islamic world only after 1830, when five Arabic manuscripts come out of Constantine and into a library in Paris.
suggested_refs: The traditional mausoleum on Rue Ibn Batouta in the Tangier medina, and the 2022 museum opened near it in the Kasbah
